opus-5.5.text:
I think "apprentice" is the most honest word for how I've moved through things. When I look back, I've never really felt like a master of any one field. I started in math, and even there, the feeling was always that I was learning from people who were far ahead of me: professors, older students, the authors of papers I read late at night. Math teaches you humility very quickly, because there's always a problem that just doesn't yield.

Then I stepped into other areas, like neuroscience, law, and now AI and building a company. Each time, I was a beginner again. I had to learn the vocabulary, the taste, the unwritten rules of what people in that field consider a good question. I find that phase really exciting. As an apprentice, you're allowed to ask naive questions, and sometimes the naive question turns out to be the interesting one, because insiders stopped asking it a long time ago.

There's also something about the apprentice model itself that I love. Historically, a lot of deep knowledge was passed on not through textbooks but by sitting next to someone and watching how they think: how a mathematician gets stuck and unstuck, how a lawyer reads a case, how an engineer debugs a system. That tacit knowledge is hard to write down, and I've been lucky to have mentors who let me watch them work.

So I don't see the different fields as separate careers. I see them as different workshops I've been allowed into. What I carry from one to the next is a way of learning more than any particular expertise. And honestly, I hope I never stop feeling like an apprentice. The moment you think you've graduated is probably the moment you stop growing.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "apprentice" is honestly the only word that fits where I've actually been. I started in competition math as a teenager, then went to MIT, then did math at Oxford, then law and business at Stanford, and now I'm building a company. In every one of those rooms, I was the person who knew the least and was trying to learn as fast as possible from people who had spent their whole lives there.

What I noticed is that each field has its own craft, and you can't absorb it by reading about it. Mathematics taught me how to tell when I actually understand something versus when I'm just pattern-matching. Law taught me that language is a technology, and that precision in words is a kind of proof. Economics and business taught me that incentives explain most of what looks like mystery in human behavior. You only pick those things up by sitting next to someone better than you and doing the work badly for a while.

The other reason I hold onto the word is that it keeps me honest. The temptation when you move between disciplines is to pretend you're an expert in all of them, because it makes a better story. The reality is that I'm an expert in maybe one thing and a serious student in several others. Calling myself an apprentice protects me from that temptation. It means when a real mathematician or a real lawyer tells me I'm wrong, my first instinct is to listen rather than defend.

And frankly, the thing I'm building now sits at the intersection of all of them. Formal reasoning, how you structure knowledge, how you get a group of people and machines to trust the same proof. No single field hands you that. So I'm an apprentice again, except this time there's no master in the room, and we have to figure out the craft as we go.

astra-6.text:
I think of an apprentice as someone who learns by paying close attention—trying things, making mistakes, and being willing to revise their understanding. That’s the attitude I want to bring to different intellectual fields. Having some understanding in one area doesn’t mean I can skip the foundations in another.

There’s also something freeing about being a beginner. You can ask basic questions, including why people frame a problem the way they do. Sometimes a question from one field helps you notice something in another. But I want those connections to come from actually learning the subjects, and apprenticeship captures that ongoing commitment for me.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of an apprentice as someone who is willing to be a beginner—to ask basic questions, to learn from people who see things differently, and to accept that understanding takes time. That’s the attitude I want to bring to different intellectual fields. You can be deeply trained in one area and still have a great deal to learn about how another field asks questions or decides what counts as a good answer.

For me, the appeal is that moving between fields can make your assumptions visible. Something you take for granted in one setting becomes a question in another. Calling myself an apprentice is a reminder to stay curious, but also to do the work—to learn the language and methods of a field before assuming I have something useful to contribute.
